source.title: Diverse Genomic Embedding Benchmark for functional evaluation across the tree of life
source.authors: Jacob A. West-Roberts; Joshua Kravitz; Nishant Jha; Andre Cornman; Yunha Hwang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether downstream task performance changes with model size or pretraining FLOPs, using biological embedding benchmarks rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study reports benchmark performance trends against model size and pretraining FLOPs. It does not test cross-entropy loss, fit power laws, or determine compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Per-model task scores are also shown in Figure 3 and Appendix F; the rows below capture the study's stated aggregate trends and exceptions. The amino-acid versus nucleic-acid comparison is not a test of scale predictability.
record.test_reason: The study benchmarks size series of protein and genomic language models (ESM2 8M–3B, ProGen2 150M–6.4B, NT 50M–2.5B) on downstream embedding tasks. It reports whether task performance rises with parameters and pretraining FLOPs, which bears on V6 in a new setting: biological sequence models. It has no loss measurements, no fits and no forecasts, so it is T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that performance saturates or fails to scale with model size on many tasks, especially those with underrepresented sequences (Archaea) or functions needing long context (biosynthetic gene clusters, operons). It does scale on most AA tasks, FLOP scaling mirrors size scaling, no single model wins everywhere, and NA models capture function poorly compared with AA models.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates biological sequence embeddings on functional downstream benchmarks rather than measuring held-out language-model cross-entropy or fitting scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by modality and task. The study also reports that mid-layer and last-layer performance differ across tasks and model types, and it reports the best of those two layers.
record.problems: The results are benchmark-task performance rather than pretraining loss or formal predictive fits. The aggregate scaling statements do not provide uncertainty estimates; task scores are shown in figures and an appendix table.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model-by-task score results are reported in Figure 3 and Appendix F and exceed the 60-row limit if catalogued separately. This record retains the text's aggregate scaling statements and its explicitly named exceptions rather than selecting representative model scores.

untested.parts: Relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss; any formal predictive fit or extrapolation of downstream performance.
No shape ablations at fixed parameter count.
No loss power laws in biological modalities.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Per-series, per-task scores showing ESM2 declining on archaeal RpoB, ESM2 3B and ProGen2-xlarge saturating or dropping below smaller models, and NT non-monotone trends
Aggregate average DGEB score versus model size and versus pretraining FLOPs

record.verdict_notes: Reader's tranche T2 changed to T3 (biological sequence LMs, embedding benchmarks, no loss). The AA task exceptions are relabelled limits_scope rather than challenges, because scaling holds on most AA tasks in the same models. NA gets challenges because the effect is absent across that whole model family. Column order in Appendix F is inferred from the header (ESM2 ×5, ESM3, ProGen2 ×4, ProtT5 ×2, NT ×5, Evo ×2). Preprint; no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and how either scales with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling of loss in other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures downstream benchmark performance against model size and pretraining FLOPs, but does not test its relationship to pretraining loss or formal prediction of downstream performance.
The study does not fit scaling exponents or compare fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, or compute-optimal splits.

It also shows saturation at the top: ESM2 3B is below 650M on BacArch (0.797 vs 0.808) and ModAC (0.131 vs 0.174), and ProGen2-xlarge is at or below large on several tasks.

relationships.condition: Most amino-acid tasks (e.g. MopB, FeFe phylogeny, EC, RpoB bacterial) in the ESM2 and ProGen2 series
relationships.reason: Scores rise with parameter count, e.g. ESM2 MopB 0.654→0.902 and FeFe 0.393→0.792 (R1, with FLOPs in R6).
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased with parameter count, including ESM2 MopB from 0.654 to 0.902 and FeFe from 0.393 to 0.792.

relationships.condition: AA tasks on multi-gene functions (MIBiG, operonic pairs) and underrepresented archaeal RpoB; saturation at the largest models
relationships.reason: Authors explicitly report no scaling on these tasks. ESM2 archaeal RpoB even declines (0.375→0.293) (R2, R3, R4, R6).
relationships.display_finding: The tested tasks showed no scaling gains, and ESM2 archaeal RpoB performance declined from 0.375 to 0.293.

relationships.reason: Authors report little to no improvement with size on NA tasks. Appendix F values are flat or declining, e.g. 16S bacterial 0.368→0.311 (R5).
relationships.display_finding: Performance stayed flat or declined across model sizes, including a decrease from 0.368 to 0.311 on the 16S bacterial task.
